items.title: Democrats won big in the midterms. Here's what they plan to do next | World News - Business Standard
items.excerpt: Democrats basking in their November 3 election wins will soon unveil an ambitious legislative agenda for the first 100 days and ​beyond, in a test of progressives' influence and Republicans' willingness to cooperate, as they take control of the US Congress on January 3. That agenda is likely to be unveiled in early December once a Senate leadership race is settled. It will mark a thunderous reversal of the past two years, when President Donald Trump's Republicans ruled the Senate and House of Representatives. With their narrow majorities, they rammed through major tax cuts skewed toward the rich and stood by as Trump grabbed their powers over tariffs and spending. Democrats' new majorities in Congress are anything but narrow. With a 56-44 majority in the Senate they are four votes short of the 60 votes needed to advance most legislation. In the House, their 257-172 force could grow beyond an 85-vote margin once a ‌handful of races are settled. ... But in a warning to Democrats, veteran Republican Senator John Boozman of ​Arkansas said in an interview that despite his party's losses across the United States, Trump remains "a powerful force" and "I don't see any of his vetoes getting overridden" by Congress during his remaining two years in office. ... For ​months, Democrats have been plotting a House-Senate coordinated attack to undo Trump's major accomplishments, according to lawmakers and aides. With the high cost of living the top concern voiced by voters, Democratic leaders are going after the low-hanging fruit that also would help unite their party's progressives and moderates. Early votes are expected on legislation handcuffing Trump's ability to wage war on Iran without Congress' approval, which would help lower gasoline prices. Reversing Republicans' deep cuts to Medicaid and SNAP food stamp programs would begin helping the poor meet healthcare and grocery costs. Meanwhile, progressives have urged raising the federal minimum wage, which is unchanged since 2009 at $7.25 per hour. Some are pushing for $20 to $25. And in response to voter ​disgust over Washington ethics breaches, one of the first bills Democrats are expected to present is one barring lawmakers from insider trading of stocks. Republicans face a bind: joining Democrats could anger Trump unless he backs measures, while stonewalling could anger voters.

items.title: Democrats signal shift on Israel as Jeffries unveils first legislative priority
items.excerpt: In an interview with The New York Times, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries set a goal of advancing legislation targeting violence in Judea and Samaria within the first 100 days of the new Congress. He also called for changes in Gaza and Judea and Samaria and urged the United States to renew its commitment to a two-state solution. Jeffries, nominated by House Democrats this week to become speaker and expected to take office in January, spoke following the party's midterm election victory, which returned both chambers of Congress to Democratic control. "What ... On Judea and Samaria, Jeffries laid out a specific timetable. "What I have made clear is that within the first 100 days, I think the most decisive step that we can take relative to the situation in the West Bank is to move the West Bank Settler Violence Protection and Prevention Act," he said. ... Jeffries said the measure would have strong support within the House Democratic Caucus and should be advanced early in the new congressional session "as a meaningful step forward to changing the conditions on the ground" and as part of the push toward "two states for two people." The proposal is part of a Democratic effort to codify sanctions targeting violence in Judea and Samaria, based on an executive order issued by former President Joe Biden that President Donald Trump revoked upon returning to the White House. The legislation would freeze assets and impose US entry restrictions on individuals involved in violence and those who assist them. It would apply to Israelis and Palestinians alike. Jeffries stopped short, however, of committing to support two more far-reaching bills he was asked about: the Block the Bombs Act, which would restrict transfers of certain weapons to Israel, and the Stop the Settlements Act, which would impose sanctions on settlement activity and prohibit imports of settlement products. "I haven't articulated a position one way or the other," he said, explaining that House Democrats would discuss which steps to pursue as a caucus.

items.excerpt: ## BTS take five at MAMA; Cortis grab Song of the Year At the 2026 MAMA Awards, held over two nights at Kyocera Dome Osaka, BTS collected five trophies including Album of the Year (“Arirang”) and Artist of the Year, while rookie boy group Cortis claimed Song of the Year with “RedRed” and four awards overall. Enhypen took Fans’ Choice of the Year for a second straight year, and BIGBANG, marking their 20th anniversary, won three.

[1] Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony (bbc.com)
Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California. Photos of the wedding on Saturday show the ceremony took place by a swimming pool with the pair standing under an arch covered in white flowers. The singer's mother, Tish Cyrus, and sister, Noah Cyrus, were in attendance, Entertainment Tonight reports. Grammy-winning Cyrus, who donned a white dress for the wedding, confirmed her engagement to the 28-year-old drummer during an interview with US TV show Good Morning America last year.
